1:
Almost every voice opens by clearing away a rabbinic identification and then failing to agree on anything else. Gill reports the view that the prophet's father was Samuel, with an etymology offered to explain the change of name, and rejects it both on the span of years and because the character of Samuel's son does not fit; he passes on the rule that a father is named only when he was an honourable man, and suggests the naming may simply distinguish this prophet from another of the name. Henry calls the identification a foolish fancy and notes drily that one rabbi nevertheless undertook very gravely to justify it. Calvin goes further and calls the rule itself frivolous, remarking how bold these expositors are in inventing a fable whenever no reason appears and then alleging it as divine truth, though he allows it probable that the fathers named were men of note. Ellicott takes the prophet's name as compounded of the two divine titles, of revelation and of nature, and observes that it was a favourite name and that nothing whatever is known of him beyond his father's, which the old Greek gives differently. Keil and Delitzsch add that the traditional accounts of his birthplace are quite unsupported, and infer from his writings only that he lived in Judah and in all probability prophesied in the city.

When he prophesied is disputed outright. Keil and Delitzsch place him among the earliest of the twelve, and argue it from the fact that a later prophet opens his own book with a sentence taken from this one. Clarke lays out the alternatives and takes the other end: some critics put him after the removal of the ten tribes; an ancient authority followed by many made him a contemporary of Hosea, on the rule that where no proof exists we should be guided by the preceding prophet whose date is better known, which Clarke says is not always a safe rule; and the Hebrews maintain that he prophesied under Manasseh, which Clarke thinks the collateral circumstances favour. Wesley places him earlier still, in the latter end of one northern reign and in the days of a king of Judah. Clarke also relays a judgment on the style, that it differs much from Hosea's and is equally poetical, elegant, perspicuous and flowing, and at the same time sublime and animated, though obscure in places, and he lays down his own reading of the whole: a double prophecy, applying in its primary sense to a plague of insects with drought and famine, and in its secondary sense to an invasion, both senses to be admitted, since some expressions will fit only the dearth and others only the war.

The four devourers are the chapter's first real crux. Clarke gives the etymology of each name, from cutting short, from multiplying, from licking, and from consuming, reports a rendering that makes them four grades of locust, and then states his own conclusion against the plain reading, that all four names denote the same insect in the successive stages of its growth. Ellicott keeps them distinct as four swarms, notes that as many as ninety sorts have been reckoned, and finds significance in the number itself, pointing to the four sore judgments threatened elsewhere and to four foreign invasions. Gill and Wesley both take them for four kinds succeeding one another. Calvin cares less about the species than the sequence: single devastations were ordinary, but four barren years running, each insect finishing what the last had left, could not be chance, and was meant as a portent that even the unwilling must notice. Henry records that many interpreters take the whole for armies of men, some making the four creatures the four monarchies that in turn oppressed the people, and that many Jewish expositors read it as a parable.
5:
Why the drunkards are summoned first is answered with unusual agreement, then pressed hardest by one voice. Gill observes the irony that men accustomed neither to waking nor to howling must do both, sober not from virtue but for want of wine. Clarke adds the agricultural fact behind it, that the devastation had cut off harvest and vintage together so that there was not wine for necessary uses, and that ruin among vines by these creatures prevents the vintage for several years after. Ellicott takes the waking as a waking from the insensibility wine causes and sharpens it into a charge: the people failed to see the hand of God in a calamity that was like an acted parable, and feasted as the revellers did while enemies stood at the gates; the thing cut off he leaves open between joy and gladness, which the old Greek gives, and the means of indulgence itself. Calvin makes the summons an argument. God derides those who laugh at his judgments, and names the drunkards because that vice was then common; the force of it is that men who had wholly suffocated their senses were nevertheless constrained to feel the loss and to wake, so that the sober had no pretext left for noticing nothing. He adds that drunkards are asleep even while awake.

The invading nation is where the readings part company. Gill takes it for a nation of locusts, so called from their numbers, as ants and conies are elsewhere called a people and a folk, and an emblem of the invaders from Babylon. Ellicott makes the philological point that the word chosen here is not the one used in that proverb but a word indicative of foreign nations and suggestive of attack, so that it covers the irrational invader and the foreign conqueror at once, and he notes that the comparison of the teeth with a lion's recurs in the Apocalypse. Wesley holds both together, an innumerable multitude of insects and perhaps a prognostic of a mighty nation soon to invade, and applies the word strong either way, to the Assyrian for courage or to the vermin, weak singly and irresistible in such numbers. Clarke thinks real locusts are meant but allows a double prophecy, and then reports the attempts to make the four creatures four attacks, four hostile powers, or four named kings, before dismissing the enterprise: of such similitudes there is no end, and the best of them is arbitrary and precarious. Calvin breaks with all of them. He refuses the common view that these verses describe the locusts more fully, and holds that a distinct judgment is recorded here, war coming upon a people already worn out with famine, his point being that God had tried every means with them in turn.

Whose vine it is divides the two who ask. Ellicott hears in the possessive a mercy remembered in wrath: God appropriates the land on which the trouble falls, so that it is his own vine and fig tree, his own people, that are afflicted, and the affliction is painful to him even though deserved. Calvin denies the figure outright. The vine here is not the church, as the same word is elsewhere; God calls everything in that land his own because he had consecrated it to himself as he had chosen the people, and the point of the phrase is accusation rather than tenderness, since vines left exposed to the spoiler prove that God no longer ruled there, the people having expelled him. Gill keeps to the plain sense, the singular standing for the plural, with the wasted vine an emblem of the coming invaders. Clarke leaves the theology alone and notices the sound, listing the plays on words in which this prophet delights. Keil and Delitzsch mark only the turn the passage takes, that the whole nation is now called to mourn over the devastation.
8:
Who is told to lament is not agreed. Gill denies that the address continues to the drunkards, reports the view that the prophet speaks to himself or to the land, notes that the Targum supplies the congregation by name, and takes it of the more religious part of the people, a chaste virgin espoused and waiting. Calvin says simply that the whole land is now addressed. Ellicott makes the land itself the figure, a virgin betrothed but not yet married who has forfeited her marriage by unworthy conduct, the Lord having been faithful and Israel not. Clarke ignores the question and attacks the translation: the rendering virgin is a very improper one here, since the word means a young woman or bride, and Hebrew has another and proper word for a virgin. On the husband Calvin explains why youth is specified, that love between young people is more tender than a later match, so that the heaviest grief available is the grief of a widow whose husband died in the flower of his age, and it is monstrous for such a widow to refrain from mourning; he adds that the word for husband means lord, one who has his wife under his protection, which is why the idols bore the same name. Wesley makes the loss a death untimely rather than a broken betrothal. Henry allows either and draws the moral from the comparison, that the more we are wedded to our creature comforts the harder it is to part with them.

The cutting off of the offerings is read as the sharpest stroke in the chapter. Gill explains the mechanics, that the one offering was of fine flour with oil and frankincense and the other of wine, so that the failure of corn and vine stopped both. Ellicott generalises it: all the outward and visible signs of communion with God are gone, a total cessation of the creatures of bread and wine, and the loss is naturally felt first by the priests. Calvin turns it into the argument he has been building, that if hunger will not move them, nor the very drunkards' distress, they might at least look at a temple standing without its daily services, and reason that God would never have let his own worship lapse had he not been grievously offended. Keil and Delitzsch supply the corrective the passage needs, that the affliction is not removed by mourning and lamentation but only through repentance and supplication, and mark the turn by which the priests are summoned to that work day and night. Clarke says only that the devastation is total and described with a striking variety of expression.

The repetition in the description of the wasted field is defended by Calvin against the charge of wordiness. He grants that all of it might have been said in one sentence and that there is nothing intricate in it, but answers that being understood was not enough: the people had to apply it to themselves and perceive that they had to do with God, and to that they were not disposed. He then puts the failure exactly, that they felt the want in the mouth, the palate, the throat and the stomach but not in the heart, and mourned as brute beasts do when hungry, without asking whence the famine came. Ellicott keeps to the three things lost and names them by their uses, the wine that gladdens, the oil that makes the face shine, the bread that strengthens. Wesley notices that the corn was eaten in its greenness and that the drought was severe enough to wither the vines outright. Gill adds a second agent beside the insects, the trampling of invading horses and the seizure of the increase as fodder. Henry gives the landscape rather than the inventory, a ground with a melancholy aspect and inhabitants in tears for what they have lost.
11:
The shame laid on the husbandmen is taken as a summons to reflection rather than a reproach for failure. Gill puts it as confusion covering men who had dunged and ploughed and sown and found the increase not answering their labour. Wesley makes the shame the occasion of an enquiry, a just cause to lament and to ask why God is so displeased with them. Calvin uses the verse to defend his own method and the prophet's. He grants that nothing new is being said and answers the charge of wordiness with a principle: heavenly teaching does not intend merely that what is said be understood, but means to penetrate the heart, and therefore the word consists not of doctrine only but of exhortations and threatenings and reproofs. The whole point, he says, is that their clamour was everywhere heard, the waste land and the famine and the many calamities complained of on every side, and yet nobody would name the author of the visitation.

The list of withered trees draws a naturalist's note from one voice and a reader's from another. Clarke supplies an observer's account of how such creatures behave in another country, collecting into compact bodies a furlong or more square and marching on, letting nothing green or juicy escape them, and he names the trees they strip, glossing the last of them as the citron. Ellicott finds a method in the order of the enumeration instead: the vine is the favourite term for the chosen people, the fig tree is the one whose life is prolonged at the dresser's intercession in the parable, the pomegranate is important enough to have given its name to an idol, and then even the palm is gone, and the apple with the lemon and citron under it, so that all joy has vanished. Gill notices that the verb rendered dried up may also be read as ashamed, the vine ashamed to be seen in such a state and to disappoint its owner. Calvin takes the whole sterility as a plain sign of wrath and states the condition he has been diagnosing all along, that insensibility is the very summit of evils, when men feel their own calamities and yet do not understand that the hand inflicting them is God's.

The turn to the priests is where the chapter changes direction. Calvin marks it explicitly as the beginning of a call to repentance: having shown them grievously afflicted, the prophet now offers a remedy near at hand if they seek God's favour, and at the same time warns that the hand is still stretched out and something worse is coming unless they anticipate it. On the opening verb he allows two readings, gird yourselves, which the mention of sackcloth just after would support, or simply hasten, a metaphorical use common enough, and judges that the drift is much the same either way. He then explains why the priests are addressed before the general exhortation that follows: those whom God has set over others must lead the way, since to pray for and further the salvation of the brethren is the common duty of all the godly and especially enjoined on ministers. Ellicott reaches the same place by a shorter route, that they are to begin preparations for a national humiliation with themselves, the visitation having touched them in a vital part by leaving them nothing to offer. Gill notes only that the girding is with sackcloth, as two Jewish commentators supply the words.
14:
The proclamation of the fast is unpacked by each voice at a different level. Gill takes the command as addressed to the priests, whose business it was to appoint such a day, keep it holy and see that others did, and passes on the reading that makes it a charge to prepare the people by giving them notice. Wesley says the same briefly, a day set apart to afflict themselves, confess their sins and sue out pardon, gathered into the courts where the people were accustomed to pray. Clarke and Ellicott both work at the word rendered solemn assembly. Clarke would translate it a time of restraint and defines it as total abstinence from food and from all secular employment, with the elders and representatives collected to confess and pray; he adds that the temple was still standing, so the prophecy came before the captivity of Judah. Ellicott notes that the word strictly means a festival day on which the people gathered and were relieved from work, that here they are summoned instead for a fast, and that the root meaning to shut or hold back allows the marginal rendering of a day of restraint. Henry works out what such a day required and why: the abstaining owns that they are unworthy of their necessary food and mortifies the body which occasioned the sin, and was seasonable now, since when God says you shall fast it is time to say we will fast. He adds that all shared the national guilt and the calamity, so all must join in the profession of repentance.

The cry that follows raises the question of who is speaking. Keil and Delitzsch decide it against the versions that supply a word of introduction: this is not what the priests are told to say but the prophet's own exclamation, justifying the appeal he has just made; the day already fallen on the land is the beginning of the approaching day of the Lord, which comes as a devastation from the Almighty and brings down everything that has exalted itself. Gill takes the coming day as heavier judgments than insects and drought, of which those were a presage, and names the destruction of city, temple and nation. Wesley makes it conditional, troubles heaped upon them unless fasting, prayer and amendment prevent. Calvin explains the phrase itself: it is called the Lord's day because in it he stretches out his hand to judge, whereas while he bears with men he seems not to rule the world at all and his face seems hidden; and the prophet says it is near to stop the procrastination of people who, even when touched by judgments, ask for time to be prolonged.

Two of them stop on the sound and the sense of the words. Clarke reports that one version repeats the opening cry and three others repeat it thrice, and takes the destruction as no ordinary calamity but a signal judgment immediately inflicted. Ellicott records the same threefold repetition and the comment it provoked, that the prophet describing the fearful sentence of an angry judge was not able to express it but stammered like a child; and he notes that the Hebrew keeps an alliteration which the translation loses, destruction from the destroyer, the title used being the one that signifies omnipotence with particular reference to the power to destroy. On the food cut off before their eyes, Calvin presses the charge he has made throughout, that they were blind in the midst of light and seeing saw nothing, and that the plainest proof was want reaching the temple, since God ought not to be defrauded of his right though mortals perish a hundred times. Keil and Delitzsch make the same connection more soberly, that joy is taken from the house because destroyed crops yield neither first-fruits nor offerings, and they quote the observation that the locust anticipates the reaper.
17:
The rotting seed is explained twice over, once by the drought and once by the insects. Gill puts both causes together: the grains sown perished under the clods for want of rain, and what did bud was cropped, so an extreme famine followed. Clarke gives the mechanism, that where the sprout had been cut off as low as possible there was no further germination and the seed rotted away. Ellicott records a translator's difficulty instead, that several words in the verse occur nowhere else, so the ancient versions vary, though he judges the received English satisfactory. Calvin draws a chronological inference from the ruined storehouses: they had no use left for them, from which he concludes the sterility had been not merely severe but long, since a failure of one or two harvests would not have brought the prophet to speak so. Wesley explains their ruin differently, the owners discouraged by the barren seasons and unwilling to repair them. Keil and Delitzsch give the closing verses plainly, without comment.

The groaning of the cattle is where the chapter's argument finally turns. Clarke hears the animals in the sound of the words themselves, the neighing and braying carried by the Hebrew, and describes the beasts wandering about for grass without knowing which way to run. Gill keeps to the cause, fodder eaten or trampled and no water. Ellicott widens it, all creation sharing the perplexity, and recalls the city where by royal decree the animals were joined to the people in a fast. Calvin makes the comparison the whole point: there is more intelligence in oxen than in this people, for the herds groan and the flocks groan while the people remain stupid; and he notices that the prophet asks a question rather than telling it as narrative, a plain statement having affected them less than an exclamation of astonishment.

The prophet's own cry is read by Calvin as an act of withdrawal. Seeing that he succeeded less than he expected, and the people touched by neither shame nor fear, he leaves them and turns to God himself, saying in effect that he will not howl as profane men do but ascribe the calamity to the judge whose hand he perceives in it. Gill says the same more simply, that these are the prophet's words, resolving to use his interest at the throne of grace whatever others do. Clarke joins him and grounds the resolution in the nature of the calamity, that only God can remove it and therefore only to him can they cry. On the fire that devoured the pastures Clarke allows either a drought or the insects, since ground they have passed over looks as though flame had consumed it, while Ellicott offers three possibilities, spontaneous combustion from the heat, fires set by people trying to exterminate the swarms, or the burnt appearance left behind. Calvin points to what makes the report unusual, that the pastures named are the cool moist uplands which stay green through the greatest heats.

The last word divides on whether the beasts really pray. Wesley says they have a voice to cry as well as an eye to look up. Ellicott sets the echo against the silence, the prophet having cried and the beasts taking up his cry while man as yet seems dumb. Gill grants the crying in their way and takes it as a rebuke to those who had no sense of the judgment and did not call on God. Calvin is the one who names the figure: this is personification and cannot properly be said of beasts, but when creatures make a noise under famine it is such calling upon God as their nature admits, as the young ravens are said to call by raising their bills; and the force is again reproach, the oxen showing the people what ought to be done after the prophets have lost their labour.
